newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Contenders claim victory amid reports of fraud.
newsitem.headline: Contenders claim victory amid reports of fraud.

text.p: Armenian President Levon Ter-Petrosyan's supporters and his main challenger both claimed victory on Monday in a presidential election marred by allegations of fraud.

The Central Election Commission said the 51-year old year old President was leading with 57 percent of the vote compared to 36 percent for former prime minister Vazgen Manukyan. The commission could not say how many votes remained to be counted.

Most returns were from provincial towns and rural areas in the rocky Caucasus state, sandwiched between Iran, Georgia, Azerbaijan, and Turkey. Officials said Manukyan was leading in the capital Yerevan, but that returns were still incomplete.

In a rambling chat with supporters shown on Armenian television, Ter-Petrosyan thanked the country for what he called a "brilliant victory" that would ensure the continuation of tough economic reforms.

But Manukyan, who won many voters with promises to drastically raise living standards in the still impoverished country, said he was the real victor and accused Ter-Petrosyan of trying to steal the election.
"We have achieved victory in the first round, regardless of massive falsification," the bespectacled 50-year old physicist told reporters at a news conference.
"But we won't let them have a false president," he added. "The people will defend their elections most resolutely."
The contest between the two former close allies, both of whom played big roles in leading Armenia to independence from the Soviet union in 1991, had grown bitter.
Sensing his rival gaining ground, Ter-Petrosyan had launched blistering attacks in the closing hours of the campaign saying that a Manukyan presidency would bring "tyranny and chaos".
Manukyan and his supporters allege massive fraud, voter intimidation, and other irregularities were being committed by Ter-Petrosyan's forces.
On Monday evening he led about 50,000 supporters in defiant evening march through central Yerevan.

Carrying red, orange, and blue Armenian flags and yelling "Vazgen President!" and "Levon out!", they snarled traffic by marching down a main street and converged on a building holding the the Central Election Commission before dispersing.
Communist Sergei Badalyan and Ashot Manucharyan of the Scientific-Industrial Citizens Union also took part in the polls but failed to win any substantial backing.
A candidate has to win a simple majority of votes cast to win the election in the first round. Otherwise a runoff vote would be held between the top two vote getters in two weeks.

International observers have backed up some of the allegations. One said he had seen a large group of soldiers being ordered to vote for Ter-Petrosyan at one polling station, and that the same group then voted again at another location.
He said it was too early to say if the legitimacy of the election was threatened.
Others said that some election officials had attempted to switch ballots or even whole ballot boxes, and that in some locations urns were stolen by Ter-Petrosyan monitors.
One monitor said unregistered voters had been able to vote wherever they wished, raising the prospect of multiple voting.

"In many of the precincts that I saw as many as a quarter of the people who voted were not on the register. This means that if they wanted too, a person could wander around voting as many times as he or she wanted," said Mark Almond, an observer from the British Helsinki Human Rights Group.
"This is clearly against the election code," he said.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which is coordinating foreign observers, is due to release a report on the conduct of the vote on Tuesday.
Hamlet Gasparyan, press secretary for Ter-Petrosyan's campaign team, dismissed the accusations of major foul play.
"There may have been some violations, but not flagrant ones. It was not enough to change the fact that the president has won," he said.
